http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/03/cuba-.text: Cuba's power grid failed on Sunday, causing another nationwide blackout, a state energy company said in a social media post.As the lights suddenly turned off across the capital Havana, residents who were sat outside to get some respite from the summer heat audibly groaned en masse.Cuba has been suffering rolling power cuts due to ageing equipment and a US energy embargo that halted regular deliveries of fuel for power stations.State-run UNE said there was a "total disconnection" of the national electricity system, plunging the country, including the capital, into abrupt darkness.This is just the latest in a series of total collapses of the electricity grid.Just 24 hours ago, the whole west of the country went dark.The power cuts have made normal life almost impossible, with each outage also meaning that water supplies trickle away and ceiling fans slow to a halt.It is a growing strain for a society used to adversity but now stuck in a months-long crisis that has no obvious end in sight.Residents in the worst-affected areas have vented their frustrations by setting piles on trash on fire or banging on pots and pans.The Ministry of Energy said that protocols to reactivate the grid were underway.Washington has authorised the arrival of only one Russian tanker, carrying 100,000 tons of crude, which came in March. Those reserves have since been exhausted.In addition to enacting an oil blockade, the Trump administration has ramped up sanctions against Cuban state-owned businesses, prompting many foreign firms to suspend operations in the country.The United States has also indicted former president Raúl Castro, brother of revolutionary leader Fidel Castro, over the downing of two civilian planes three decades ago.Talks between Havana and Washington appear to have made little in the way of progress.Havana has enacted a series of free-market reforms to give the economy a boost.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: The US navy Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS George Washington transits the strait of Malacca on 13 August. Photograph: US Navy/Reuters View image in fullscreen The US navy Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS George Washington transits the strait of Malacca on 13 August. Photograph: US Navy/Reuters US military US aircraft carrier arrives in Middle East to relieve troubled USS Lincoln USS George Washington will replace warship families say suffers from shortages, plumbing problems and low morale Anna Betts Thu 20 Aug 2026 14.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 14.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The USS George Washington aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East, where it is expected to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln from its record deployment amid concerns about poor living conditions and morale. US Central Command announced on Thursday that the Washington arrived in the area on Wednesday, and posted an image of sailors working on the flight deck as the ship transited the Arabian Sea. No date has yet been announced for the Lincoln to return to the US. In an interview this week, the wife of a sailor onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln told the Guardian that she has been getting brief glimpses over the past few months of what life is like on the aircraft carrier, mostly through text messages. And that as the deployment has stretched on, and on, she has noticed a change in her husband’s messages. “There’s less hope in the way he talks and less positive things that he has to say,” she said. “You can just tell the little things. “He’s just exhausted,” she added. “It’s a long, long deployment and it takes a toll.” The woman, who spoke on the condition of anonymity out of fear of retribution, said that her husband rarely complained. But photographs he sent of what she described as his sometimes sparse meals as supplies ran low have left her worried. One meal she described as just a “couple of pieces of bacon and three or four chicken wings”. “He’s never complaining. It’s just when I ask him a question, I’m like, OK, wait a minute, that’s not right,” she said. “To put it plainly, I just don’t think they’re getting enough calories.” To put it plainly, I just don’t think they’re getting enough calories Her account comes as recent reports have rung alarm bells about conditions onboard the Lincoln, which has spent more than 250 days at sea supporting US operations against Iran without a significant port visit or date to return home for the 5,000 sailors aboard. Reports from families of crew members published in the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes military newspapers described food and water shortages, disrupted mail services, plumbing problems, low morale and worsening mental health, prompting Democratic lawmakers to demand answers from the Pentagon. “I just don’t really think they’re treating them like people. I think they’re treating them like a uniform, like a pawn on a chessboard,” the wife said in a telephone interview. Over the weekend, Adm Brad Cooper of US Central Command visited the ship, and released a statement saying the Lincoln “currently has among the lowest number of cases related to mental health” of the navy’s 11 active aircraft carriers, but acknowledged “that doesn’t mean all is perfect”, describing long deployments at sea as “uniquely challenging and tough”. A navy official, in a statement last week, also recognized that the war had disrupted traditional supply hubs, but said that “current reports from the ship confirm continuous access to clean water, functional [air conditioning] and healthy meal options”. But the wife of the sailor still worries for her husband and his shipmates. “He has not point-blank said anything, but I feel like I can tell through text it’s getting hard … being deployed without having any stops, and just kind of doing the same thing over and over again for months is exhausting,” she said, adding: “especially when you’re dealing with high stress” in a war zone. The couple are in their early 20s and he works on the planes on the flight deck. She said her husband told her that morale among some sailors was low, and that they had been unable to receive packages from home for some time, but she believes the sailors are reluctant to speak out because they fear the consequences for their careers. “It’s not the sailors that are complaining. It’s their family members who are saying: ‘Whoa, whoa, whoa.’ They are the ones putting their foot down,” she said. Carl Otis Schuster, a retired US navy captain, said he thought more attention should be paid to the “human element” of these deployments, adding that “until we do that, you’re going to have repeats” of the kinds of problems that have emerged. “Unfortunately, we’ve made a habit of placing the sacrifices on the crewmen,” Schuster said. “Every generation says that this generation is soft, but I would argue the guys serving on the Abraham Lincoln have undergone stresses and strains that my generation rarely faced, and certainly I never faced.” Schuster served for 26 years on various US and allied warships. The Lincoln’s crew, he said, had “shown really strong resilience”. During his own service, he said, he never spent more than 90 days at sea, and warned: “All of us have a breaking point.” He said that typically about 70% of the crew on a ship like the Lincoln are age 26 or younger, living and working together in a confined space. “We have one carrier fulfilling the mission that would normally be done by two, so there’s nowhere to rotate them out, and so the tension and stress on the crew grows,” he said. Asked about Donald Trump’s comments last Friday that the Lincoln’s deployment was “ not nearly long enough ”, Schuster said that the US president may be correct strategically that the US needs a carrier in the region for longer, but that the statement “ignores the human element”, which he said was “everything”. Lory Manning, who served more than 25 years in the navy, said that sailors typically leave for deployments with a sense of when they will be returning and that “every time that is changed, it’s demoralizing”. Aircraft carriers, she said, were noisy, crowded and constantly operating. Sailors often work long hours, some in warm areas of the ship such as the engine room, where “you might not get much daylight”, and shortages of basic supplies can make prolonged deployments even harder. “There’s no privacy,” she said. “In a sense, [it can ultimately feel like] you’re in a jail because you’re on this ship and you can’t get off.” Yet Manning, who after retiring from the navy got involved with work centered on female veterans and women in the military, said that sailors continued to do their jobs despite the strains. “The work is getting done, the people are doing what they’re supposed to do,” she said. Still, she wonders what the long-term consequences may be. “How many of them will re-enlist someday?” she said. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: People in the EU have been encouraged to have a crisis pack including bottled water, a transistor radio, canned food and cash. Photograph: Sakis Mitrolidis/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen People in the EU have been encouraged to have a crisis pack including bottled water, a transistor radio, canned food and cash. Photograph: Sakis Mitrolidis/AFP/Getty Images European Union Anxiety over war, wildfires and cyber-attacks leads to growth in cash stocks in EU Value of banknotes in circulation rises from €1bn in 2016 to €1.6bn in 2026 as people advised to keep stash of cash Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent Fri 21 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 00.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The number of banknotes in circulation in the EU is increasing despite widespread smartphone payments, new data shows, with wildfires ripping through parts of Europe fuelling demand for an emergency stash of cash. While cash plays second fiddle to contactless payments in many cities across Europe, the amount in circulation is actually going up, Philip Lane, the chief economist of the European Central Bank (ECB), said at the MacGill summer school conference in Ireland. The rise of cash has been linked to anxiety over wars and the impact of cyber-attacks on online and contactless payment systems, say experts. “The total stock of banknotes is continuing to grow. In transactions, it [the number of notes] is coming down, but in terms of the stock [it is increasing],” Lane said. Last year Marks & Spencer in the UK suffered a sustained cyber-attack which stopped the retailer taking online orders for weeks. In 2025 EU residents were advised to stockpile enough food, water and essentials for 72 hours in case of an emergency such as this summer’s catastrophic wildfires in France and Spain, floods or storms as well as potential cyber-attacks or other hostile events. Households were encouraged to have a crisis pack including bottled water, a transistor radio, canned food and, critically, cash. ECB data, which has been tracking the number of bank notes in circulation since 2002, shows that their has gone up from about €1bn in 2016 to €1.6bn in June 2026. More than 31m notes are in circulation compared with 24m just before the pandemic in 2019, with the €50 note the most popular in 2025 followed by the €100. European countries including Austria, Finland, Germany, Sweden and the Netherlands have already recommended that citizens keep between €70 and €100 per household, enough to pay for essentials for 72 hours should online and mobile apps go down. In a “use it or lose it” warning, Olive McCarthy, professor at University College Cork with an interest in financial inclusion, said the continued use of cash was vital for society. “While advice to maintain cash for emergencies is well made, and serves to remind us all to be prepared when digital systems let us down, it is essential that cash does not become viewed merely as a backup measure. If we stop using it when there isn’t a crisis, it might not be easy to use it when there is.” The ECB says cash is a critical part of “national crisis preparedness”, describing its shrinking use for day-to-day purchases amid an increase in people keeping banknotes as a “paradox”. Lane also referenced the need for legislation to ensure networks of cash machines remain a feature of every high street across the EU. “Some consumers prefer the privacy and convenience of cash. We are also seeing more talk about the importance of cash in a crisis,” said McCarthy, pointing to the fact it was “inclusive”, available to elderly and vulnerable citizens including victims of domestic abuse who may depend on cash if their partner is controlling their spending. It was also a great tool to help children with financial literacy and budgeting, she added. https://www.ewtnnews.com/vatican/10-year.text: 10 years after Amoris Laetitia , bishops to discuss challenges of families at the Vatican Vatican officials said the weeklong meeting is neither a synod, nor an evaluation of Amoris Laetitia. Jesuit Father Giacomo Costa, Gabriella Gambino, and Orietta Rachele Grazioli speak to journalists during a press conference on Oct. 2, 2026, about a meeting on Amoris Laetitia to be held Oct. 7–14, 2026, at the Vatican. | Credit: Victoria Cardiel/EWTN News By Victoria Cardiel · Vatican Bureau Follow + October 2, 2026 at 1:00 PM ET Pope Leo XIV has convened a gathering on the family at the Vatican from Oct. 7–14, during which bishops will listen to the testimony of 11 married couples from five continents. These families will present to more than 150 bishops the challenges they encounter in passing on the faith in increasingly secularized societies. The meeting is being organized on the occasion of the 10th anniversary of Amoris Laetitia , the postsynodal apostolic exhortation published by Pope Francis in 2016. The document sparked intense debate, especially after the bishops of the Buenos Aires Pastoral Region interpreted it as allowing, following a process of accompanied pastoral discernment, access to the sacraments of reconciliation and the Eucharist for some Catholics who are divorced and civilly remarried “when a person judges that he or she would fall into a further fault by harming the children of the new union.” In 2023, the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith confirmed that this interpretation forms part of the authentic magisterium after being incorporated into the Acta Apostolicae Sedis , the Holy See’s official bulletin. According to the Dicastery for the Laity, the Family, and Life, participants in the meeting will include the heads of the 15 Eastern Catholic Churches “sui iuris” (14 represented by their patriarchs or highest authorities and one by a delegate), the presidents of the world’s 115 bishops’ conferences (those of Peru, Paraguay, Turkey, and Ethiopia will send delegates), two representatives of bishops from territories without a bishops’ conference, and 22 participants specially chosen by the Holy Father. In addition, 67 other people will attend, including members of the Dicastery for the Laity, the Family, and Life, the General Secretariat of the Synod, and 26 experts and 16 facilitators. Not an evaluation of Amoris Laetitia During a presentation of the gathering at the Vatican, Gabriella Gambino, undersecretary of the Dicastery for the Laity, the Family, and Life since 2017, a laywoman, mother of five, and doctor of bioethics, emphasized that “this is not about evaluating a text but about deepening our understanding of the family and pastoral realities that have received and interpreted this document in different ways, just as the life of the Church is diverse in the various places around the world where it is present and rooted in the one Gospel.” “The central point on which we must focus our attention is that the Church’s goal is not to see texts applied mechanically and uniformly in every reality, because each one has characteristics that are very different from the others,” she said. She stated that the central question of the meeting is: “How is the faith transmitted today? How is faith passed on in families today, and how do families contribute to building up the Church?” “Without families, the Church cannot renew its Christian roots. It is in families that children are born, where faith and values are transmitted, for better or worse, and where vocations arise,” she explained. To illustrate the scale of the ongoing religious changes, Gambino offered several statistics. In Poland, religious marriages celebrated over the last five years have declined by 45%. In Australia, they have fallen from 88% in 1970 to 16% in 2024. In her view, these are signs that, in different contexts, highlight the urgency of better accompanying couples in their decision to marry and providing stronger support for the transmission of faith within the family. Orietta Rachele Grazioli, a tenured professor of canon law and comparative family law at the Pontifical John Paul II Theological Institute for Marriage and Family Sciences, and vice coordinator of the expert group, explained that the “methodology chosen by the Holy Father for this gathering is centered on two key words that complement one another: listening and discernment.” 5 major themes The gathering will be structured around five major themes related to marriage, family life, and the transmission of the faith. Reflection will begin with “Families Today: Reality, Beauty, and Challenges,” dedicated to analyzing the current situation of the family, and will continue with “Young People and the Discovery of the Vocation to Marriage,” “Married Life: The First Years of Marriage, a Decisive Time,” and “In Life’s Difficulties: Accompanying and Supporting,” which will address the accompaniment of engaged and married couples at different stages of their journey. The meeting will conclude with the theme “Christian Families as Subjects of the Church’s Mission,” focused on the evangelizing role of families and their contribution to ecclesial life. Father Giacomo Costa, a consultant to the General Secretariat of the Synod, said that “the question is not what Amoris Laetitia says but what we have learned by trying to live it.” He also recalled that the goal identified by Pope Leo XIV, who will be present at both the opening and closing of the gathering, is “to advance in mutual listening toward a synodal discernment about the steps we must take today to proclaim the Gospel with families. The composition of the assembly itself reflects this objective.” Before the start of the proceedings, an introductory meditation will be given by Sister Helen Alford, president of the Pontifical Academy of Social Sciences. Each morning will be structured around three types of speeches: family testimonies, contributions from bishops, and reflections from experts. ‘The goal is not to eliminate differences’ “The goal is not to eliminate differences. We do not want to arrive at an artificial consensus,” Costa said. Each day will include a report summarizing the discussions, which will serve as the basis for extensive dialogue and debate sessions in the afternoon. He made clear, however, that “this is not a new synod on the family but a process guided by the synodal method, one that consciously draws upon the experience of the synods and other forums of the Church.” Regarding the expected outcomes of the gathering, Costa insisted that “nothing has been predetermined.” A final summary will be prepared at the conclusion of the assembly, but no concluding document will be published. The text will be reviewed by a commission tasked with verifying that it faithfully reflects what emerged during the working sessions. Afterward, the presidents of bishops’ conferences will be invited to promote initiatives in their local Churches aimed at opening new pastoral paths and further developing the proposals that emerge from the gathering.
